Part 1: Forces, Moments, and Static Equilibrium
Definitions
Mass
A scalar (described with magnitude and not with direction) property of a physical body that is
reflected by its resistance to acceleration if a force is applied
The Standard International (SI) unit of mass is kilograms (kg).
Acceleration
The rate at which the velocity of an object changes with time
Acceleration has the SI unit of meters per second squared (m/s2) and is a vector quantity
(described with magnitude and direction).
Force
Any interaction on an object that, if unopposed, will change the motion of an object
Importantly, force is a vector quantity—it has a magnitude and a direction.
The SI unit of force is newtons (N).
Because force = mass × acceleration, 1 N = 1 kg m/s2

Definitions
The force of gravity on earth equals the product of the mass of the object (in kg) and the
acceleration of gravity of the earth at its surface (9.8 m/s2). This product gives the weight
of the object in newtons. As a matter of convenience, weight (which is a force) is
commonly reported in kg because the acceleration of gravity on the earth’s surface is
constant. On the earth’s surface, it makes some sense to report weight in kilograms as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
2/30

an object with 1 kg of mass weighs 1 kg of force. However, it makes no sense to report
weight in kilograms on the moon. On the moon, because the acceleration of gravity is
much less than on earth, a mass of 1 kg weighs less than 1 kg. The mass does not
change, but the weight does.
Resultant Force
The resultant force is the vector sum of the forces being applied to the object.

Resultant Force
If multiple forces are acting on a body, they can be added to determine a resultant force.
Because force is a vector, the magnitude and the direction must be accounted for. The
common method to add forces is with head-to-tail addition of the force vectors.
Moment and Moment Arm
Moment arm is the distance between the site of the applied force and the location about
which the moment is being calculated.
Moment arm has an SI unit of distance (meters).
Moment is the product of the force and the moment arm and has a direction (clockwise or
counterclockwise).
Moment has an SI unit of Nm.

Moment and Moment Arm
A moment is defined in relation to a fixed point in space. A force applied at a distance
from that fixed position creates a moment about that point that is calculated by
multiplying the magnitude of the force by the shortest perpendicular distance to the
point, which is known as the moment arm. Moment arm has an SI unit of distance
(meters), and moment, therefore, has an SI unit of newton meters (Nm). It is important
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
3/30

to note that moments have directionality as they can cause objects to spin in a particular
direction. Moments are commonly thought of as being in the clockwise or
counterclockwise direction about a particular fixed point in space (from our reference
perspective). Torque is a commonly used term that has the same meaning as moment in
physics.
Resultant Moment
Like vectors, moments can be added. The direction of the moment needs to be noted.

Resultant Moment
If adding moments about a certain point, the direction of the moments needs to be
noted. The resultant moment is the sum of the individual moments that are being
applied about a fixed point in space at the same time.
Mass Moment of Inertia
Mass moment of inertia is a property of a physical body that reflects its resistance to angular
acceleration if a moment is applied.

Mass Moment of Inertia
Force (F) = mass × acceleration. This applies to a force pushing and accelerating a mass
in a straight line. If the force is applying a moment about the center of mass of the
object, then the object will spin. In this case, moment = mass moment of inertia ×
angular acceleration. Objects of the same mass may be more difficult to spin if their
mass is distributed far from the center of mass (eg, a flywheel). A flywheel is hard to
begin turning because it has a high mass moment of inertia.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
4/30

Free Body Diagram
A free body diagram can be used to analyze the effects of forces and moments on an object.

Free Body Diagram
To determine how an object will move in space if multiple forces and moments are being
applied to it, it is helpful to draw a free body diagram of the object. At the edges of the
object of interest, all the externally applied forces (as vectors) and moments (including
directions) being applied to the object are drawn. This affords easier visualization with
regard to what is happening to the object and allows for calculation of the resultant
forces and moments to determine if or how the object will move. A very simple free body
diagram is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1 Illustration shows a free body diagram of a seesaw. The external forces (weights
of the two children and the ground reaction force) and their locations on the free body
are shown. (Reproduced from Mow VC, Flatow EL, Foster RJ: Biomechanics, in Simon SR,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
5/30

ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 1994, p 404.)
Degrees of Freedom
An object that is unconstrained and floating freely in space will have six degrees of freedom.
External constraints to movement will reduce the degrees of freedom.

Degrees of Freedom
At maximum, if motion is unconstrained for an object, an object can have six degrees of
freedom. It can move linearly in the three directions in space (anatomically this could be
to the right or left, anteriorly or posteriorly, and superiorly or inferiorly). The object also
can rotate around three different axes (anatomically, this would be rotation in the
coronal plane, the sagittal plane, and the axial plane). In most biomechanical situations
motion is constrained and has fewer than six degrees of freedom. For example, the
femur in an idealized hip joint has no translational degrees of freedom but can rotate in
three planes. The hip can flex and extend, abduct and adduct, and internally and
externally rotate. Therefore, it has three degrees of freedom.
Static Equilibrium
If all the externally applied forces and moments on an object add up to zero, then the object is
in static equilibrium—it will not move.

Static Equilibrium
The seesaw shown in Figure 1 is in static equilibrium. The moments and the forces on
the seesaw balance. Starting with the moments, the child on the left generates a 600-Nm
moment about the pivot point in the counterclockwise direction. The child on the right
generates a 600-Nm moment about the pivot point in the clockwise direction. These two
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
6/30

moments balance and, therefore, the seesaw will not rotate. Moving on to the forces, the
child on the left pushes down on the seesaw with 600 N of force. The child on the right
pushes down on the seesaw with 300 N of force. The ground must then be pushing up
on the seesaw with 900 N of force. The downward 900 N of force is opposed by an
upward 900 N of force. The moments and forces on the seesaw are balanced, and the
seesaw is in static equilibrium.
Illustrative Example of Using a Free Body Diagram and Assuming Static
Equilibrium to Determine the Joint Reaction Force in a Hip
The following exercise will demonstrate the use of a free body diagram in an orthopaedic
application.
The goal is to determine the joint reaction force of a hip in a patient who is in single leg stance.
To simplify the analysis, static equilibrium can be assumed (Figure 2, A).
First, a free body diagram needs to be created. The free body in this situation is the body above
the right hip. To simplify matters, the body above the right hip can be assumed to weigh 1 body
weight (BW). The center of mass can be assumed to be located at the midline of the patient. The
right leg is anchored to the ground and does not move. The body above the right hip tips side to
side (in this plane) around the pivot point at the center of the right hip. Although it does not
appear similar, the body above the right hip is similar to the seesaw shown in Figure 1 and also
can tip side to side about a pivot point. The seesaw can be drawn on a radiograph to allow for
easier analysis. The known body weight force is placed on the free body diagram. The other
forces acting on the free body are the hip abductor force, which is pulling the pelvis down on its
side of the seesaw, and the joint reaction force, which is pushing up on the seesaw at the pivot
point (Figure 2, B). The body weight is known. The hip abductor force and the joint reaction force
are unknown.
The first step in solving this problem is to balance the moments about the hip joint. The body
weight moment arm is 2x, so the moment applied by the body weight force about the hip joint is
equal to BW times 2x. This moment is applied in a clockwise direction about the center of the hip
joint. The joint reaction force does not apply a moment about the pivot point because the
moment arm for the joint reaction force is zero. Therefore, only one other moment is being
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
7/30

applied to this seesaw, which is the moment being applied by the hip abductors. The abductor
moment arm is x. Since static equilibrium exists, the moments about the pivot point must
balance. A clockwise moment of 2xBW is applied to the seesaw, so the abductor moment must
be 2xBW in the counterclockwise direction. If this is the case, then the abductor force must be
2BW (Figure 2, C). This is exactly the same situation as that observed in the seesaw shown in
Figure 1, in which one child weighed twice as much as the other and was positioned half as far
from the pivot point.
The moments are balanced, and the seesaw is not tipping in the clockwise or counterclockwise
direction. A total force being is applied to the seesaw in the downward direction of three times
body weight. Therefore, the joint reaction force must be three times body weight in the upward
direction. (Figure 2, D)
Figure 2 AP radiographs of the right hip of a patient demonstrate how to determine the joint
reaction force of the hip. A, Radiograph obtained with the patient in single leg stance and static
equilibrium. B, Radiograph with the free body diagram superimposed. The body above the right
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
8/30

hip joint is similar to a seesaw that pivots about the hip joint, similar to the seesaw shown in
Figure 1. The patient’s body weight is attempting to tip the seesaw down on one side. The
abductor force is pulling the pelvis (and, therefore, the rest of the body) down on its side of the
seesaw. The joint reaction force is pushing the free body up at the hip center of rotation. C,
Radiograph with the free body diagram superimposed. The abductor moment arm is 2× body
weight because it is being applied half as far from the pivot point as the body weight force on the
other side of the pivot. D, Radiograph with the free body diagram superimposed. A joint reaction
force of 3× body weight results in static equilibrium. The sum of the moments and the sum of the
forces on the free body equal zero. (Images courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Part 2: Mechanics of Materials
Isotropic Material
A material that has the same material properties in all directions

Isotropic Material
This is an idealized situation; however, examples in orthopaedics would be metals,
plastics, and ceramics.
Anisotropic Material
A material that has material properties that depend on the direction that the force is applied

Anisotropic Material
All biologic tissues are anisotropic as the structural elements, such as collagen fibers,
have directionality. Tendon is a great example of an anisotropic material. It is stiff if it is
pulled in the direction of the collagen fibers and less stiff if it is pulled in a different
direction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
9/30

Strain
Strain is the change in length divided by the original length of an object that has deformed
under load.
Strain is a unitless quantity (meters/meters) and is commonly presented as a percentage.

Strain
A 10% strain indicates that the elongation of the object is equal to 10% of the resting
length of the object. Strain within the substance of a material is a three-dimensional
quantity (a tensor). What is described above is the strain in a particular direction.
Stress
Stress is the force applied over a unit of area.
The SI unit of stress is the pascal (Pa).
Because stress is defined as force over area, 1 pascal equals 1 newton per meter squared (1 Pa
= 1 N/m2).

Stress
The easiest way to envision stress is to think about pressure. Pressure is compressive
stress applied over a unit of area; however, stress can be tensile, shear, or a
combination. Shear stress results from a force that runs parallel to the surface, whereas
compressive and tensile stresses are applied perpendicular (or normal) to the surface
(hence known as normal stresses). Stress within the substance of a material is a three-
dimensional quantity (a tensor). What is described above is the stress applied to a
surface of a material.
Toughness
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
10/30

The toughness of a material is the energy per unit volume that it can absorb before it breaks.
On the stress-strain curve, the toughness is represented by the area under the stress-strain
curve.
Force-Displacement Curve
A force-displacement curve describes the deformation of a particular object under load.

Force-Displacement Curve
If a mechanical test was performed on the deformation of an object under load, the
object would be put into a machine that can apply a force to the object and measure
displacement of the surface of the object (deformation). The result of this test would be
a force-displacement curve (Figure 3). The vertical axis of the force displacement curve is
the force applied to the object. The horizontal axis is the displacement of the surface of
the object. As can be seen in Figure 3, the more force that is applied, the greater the
deformation of the object. In this hypothetical situation, the relationship of force and
displacement remains linear initially, then the slope of the line reduces before the object
eventually breaks (represented by the end of the line). A force-displacement curve is
useful to obtain information about the deformation of a specific structure or object;
however, it is associated with the disadvantage of being dependent on the material
properties of the object and the geometry of the object. Objects that are made of the
same material but have different cross-sectional areas, for example, will have different
force-displacement curves.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
11/30

Figure 3 Image shows the force-displacement curve (left) of a specimen (right). The curve
reflects the mechanical behavior of the specimen if it is loaded in tension. (Left image
courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA. Right image reproduced from Mow
VC, Flatow EL, Foster RJ: Biomechanics, in Simon SR, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 1994, p 420.)
Stress-Strain Curve
A stress-strain curve describes the mechanical behavior of a material under load.

Stress-Strain Curve
In a stress-strain curve (Figure 4), the axes of the force-displacement curve are
normalized to remove any geometric considerations and assess only material (rather
than object) deformation. The vertical axis (force) is divided by the cross-sectional area of
the object, which is stress. The horizontal axis (displacement, or change in length) is
divided by the original length of the object, which is strain. The resulting stress-strain
curve has the same features as the force-displacement curve, but the curve now
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
12/30

represents only the material properties of the object and not the geometry of the object.
From this curve, many important material properties can be visualized.
Figure 4 Graph shows a typical stress-strain curve. Hooke’s law describes the linear
portion of the curve in the elastic region. (Image courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD,
Palo Alto, CA.)
Elastic Deformation and Plastic Deformation
Elastic deformation occurs in the linear portion of the stress-strain curve.
Material that is deformed elastically will return to its original shape if the load is released.
Plastic deformation occurs if the material is stressed beyond the yield strength of the material.
If an object is plastically deformed, the deformation is permanent, and releasing the load will
not return the object to its original shape.

Elastic Deformation and Plastic Deformation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
13/30

Two different regions are present in the stress-strain curve—the elastic region and the
plastic region (Figure 4). The elastic region demonstrates the material deforming
elastically. It is called elastic deformation because the deformation will return to zero in
this region of the curve if the applied stress to the material is released. In other words,
no permanent deformation of the material occurs. Conversely, in the plastic region of
the curve, the material exhibits plastic deformation. This means that the material is
being permanently deformed and will not return to its original shape if the load is
released. A simple example would be to think of a paperclip. If a paperclip is flicked with
a finger, it will briefly deform and then spring back to its original shape. This creates low
stresses in the metal of the paperclip and low strains. If the stress is released, the
paperclip returns to its normal shape, and the strain in the material returns to zero. This
deformation is elastic. If you bend the paperclip and then let go and the paperclip
remains bent, plastic deformation of the paperclip occurs.
Modulus of Elasticity and Hooke’s Law
The modulus of elasticity of the material is reflected by the slope of the line in the elastic linear
region of the stress-strain curve (Figure 4).
The modulus of elasticity has an SI unit of pascals (Pa).

Modulus of Elasticity and Hooke's Law
A stiffer material will have a steeper slope and a higher modulus of elasticity. A softer
material will have a less steep slope and a lower modulus of elasticity. The modulus of
elasticity is the slope of the curve. The slope of the curve (and the modulus of elasticity)
equals stress divided by strain. The modulus of elasticity has the units of stress (Pascals)
because strain is unitless. Hooke’s law is the equation of the line in the elastic region.
Stress equals the modulus of elasticity times the strain.
Yield Strength
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
14/30

The yield strength of a material is the stress at which the material transitions from elastic to
plastic deformation.

Yield Strength
Stressing the material below the yield strength results in no permanent deformation.
Stressing the material above the yield strength results in permanent deformation.
Ultimate Strength
The ultimate strength of a material is the stress at which the material breaks. It is represented
by the end of the line in the stress-strain curve.
Brittle Materials Versus Ductile Materials
Brittle materials exhibit no plastic deformation before breaking.
Ductile materials exhibit large plastic deformation before breaking.

Brittle Materials Versus Ductile Materials
Materials can behave differently under load. Brittle materials exhibit no plastic
deformation. Ceramics are brittle. Ceramic cannot be permanently bent or dented; it just
breaks (Figure 5, A).
Ductile materials can exhibit large plastic deformation before breaking (Figure 5, B).
Many metals are ductile. A paperclip can be tied into a knot or bent, and a plate can be
permanently deformed to fit a patient’s anatomy. Ductile materials will deform and
remain intact well before they break.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
15/30

Figure 5 Graphs show stress-strain curves. A, Graph shows the stress-strain curve for a
brittle material (blue line) compared with a material with elastic and plastic deformation
(white line). The brittle material is stiffer than the comparison material. B, Graph shows
the stress-strain curve for a ductile material (orange line). The ductile material is less stiff
than the comparison material (white line) and exhibits much plastic deformation before
breaking. (Images courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Elasticity Versus Viscoelasticity
Elastic deformation is not time-dependent.
Viscoelastic deformation is time-dependent.

Elasticity Versus Viscoelasticity
Elastic materials return to their original shape if they are unloaded. Another important
feature of elastic materials is that their deformation is not time-dependent. If an
instantaneous load is applied to an elastic material and released, the peak strain
(deformation) of the material will be the same as if the material is loaded and the load is
maintained forever. Conversely, strain of a viscoelastic material under mechanical
loading is time-dependent. Importantly, all biologic materials are viscoelastic. If a tissue
is loaded for an instant and the load is released, the tissue will deform a certain amount
in that instant of loading. If that same load is applied for an extended period of time,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
16/30

peak deformation (strain) of the tissue will occur at a later time and will be greater than
the instantaneous strain that occurred at the time of loading.
Creep and Stress Relaxation
Creep and stress relaxation are exhibited by viscoelastic materials.
Creep represents the deformation of a viscoelastic material that occurs over time.
Stress relaxation occurs if a material is elongated and held in an elongated position over time.
Initially the stress is high; however, over time, the stress in the material reduces.

Creep and Stress Relaxation
The strain (or deformation) of a viscoelastic material over time under a constant load is
called creep (Figure 6). If the viscoelastic material is stretched to a fixed distance and
held at that fixed distance for an extended period of time, the stress in the material
gradually reduces as the material stretches out internally. This is called stress relaxation.
Creep and stress relaxation reflect the time-dependent material behavior of viscoelastic
materials. In orthopaedics, creep and stress relaxation may explain why soft-tissue
repair or reconstruction are sometimes noted to stretch out and become less tight over
time.
Because tissues are viscoelastic, the deformation of tissues varies depending on the rate
of loading. A load that is applied suddenly will cause the tissue to appear stiffer and
deform less before it breaks. Conversely, if the same load is applied slowly, the tissue will
appear less stiff and deform more before it breaks. This has relevance to ligament
injuries and fracture patterns. Rapidly applied loads cause more fracture comminution
and will tend to cause tendon or ligament avulsions rather than ruptures within the
substance of the tendon or ligament.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
17/30

Figure 6 Image shows creep in a thought experiment. Imagine hanging a tendon from
the ceiling and applying a weight to the end of the tendon. The tendon will immediately
elongate a certain distance. This is the elastic component of the tendon’s deformation. If
the weight is left attached to the end of the tendon and observed the next day, the
tendon will have elongated even further than that observed immediately after applying
the weight. This additional deformation, which is time-dependent, is called creep. (Image
courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Part 3: Mechanics of Simple Structures
Area Moment of Inertia
Area moment of inertia is a purely geometric quantity that is important for determining how a
structure will bend if it is loaded.

Area Moment of Inertia
Imagine trying to bend a plate in one direction, then trying to bend the plate in the
perpendicular direction (Figure 7). It is the same plate; however, the stiffness of the
plate to bending changes depending on the direction the plate is being bent. The area
moment of inertia is the geometric property of the plate that explains this phenomenon.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
18/30

The area moment of inertia is an important geometric quantity that influences the
deformation of a structure under load. It is purely geometric and has nothing to do with
material properties. The area moment of inertia for an object is calculated from the
cross-sectional shape of the object and depends on the direction of loading. The
stiffness of a structure to bending or torsion is proportional to the bending or torsional
(polar) moment of inertia in that direction.
Figure 7 Image shows a plate, which is much easier to bend in direction B because the
area moment of inertia for bending in that direction is lower. (Image courtesy of Nicholas
J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA.)
The plate imagined above is shaped similar to a beam. The deformation of a beam
depends on the cross-sectional geometry of the beam and the direction of loading. In
Figure 8, A, imagine that the rectangular and circular shapes are cross-sections of
beams. The beam can be bent by applying a downward force to the end of the beam.
The area moment of inertia of the rectangular cross-section of the beam is shown in the
Figure 8, A. It is proportional to the height of the beam to the third power. In a beam
with a circular cross-section, the area moment of inertia of the beam is proportional to
the radius to the fourth power. Similarly, in an attempt to twist the circular cross-
sectional beam, the polar moment of inertia of the beam is proportional to the fourth
power of the radius (Figure 8, B) These are powerful effects. For example, if a Kirschner
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
19/30

wire is used to maintain fracture reduction, a 0.062-in Kirschner wire has a stiffness that
is 36 times greater than the next smaller 0.045-in Kirschner wire.
Figure 8 Images show the moment of inertia. A, Image shows the area moment of
inertia of a rectangular cross-section and a circular cross-section beam. The can be bent
by applying a downward force to the end of the beam. The rectangular cross-section
beam has a height (h). The area moment of inertia of this beam being bent in this
direction is proportional to the third power of the height. The area moment of inertia of
the circular cross-section beam is proportional to the radius of the beam to the fourth
power. B, Image shows the polar moment of inertia. Imagine twisting a beam of circular
cross-section (applying torsion to the beam). The angular deflection of the beam will be
proportional to the polar moment of inertia. The polar moment of inertia of a circular
cross-section beam also is proportional to the fourth power of the radius. (Images
courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Deflection of a Cantilever Beam
Many orthopaedic constructs can be thought of as cantilever beams.
The deflection of a cantilever beam is proportional to the force applied and the cube of the
length of the beam. It is inversely proportional to the area moment of inertia of the beam and
the modulus of elasticity of the beam material.

Deflection of a Cantilever Beam
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:58 PM
AAOS | Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002107
20/30

A cantilever beam is fixed at one end and is free to move at the other end. In
orthopaedics, locking screws, cephalomedullary nail hip screws, and the pins of an
external fixator are examples of cantilever beam-like constructs. If these constructs are
used to fix fractures, an understanding of the bending mechanics of cantilever beams is
useful (Figure 9). The deflection of the end of a cantilever beam is proportional to the
force applied and the cube of the length of the beam, and is inversely proportional to the
elastic modulus of the material and the moment of inertia of the beam. Therefore, in
fixing a fracture with the use of a uniaxial external fixator, reducing the distance
between the external fixator frame and the bone will have a great effect (third power of
the distance) on the deflection of the pins and the overall stiffness of the construct.
Figure 9 Image shows the deflection of a cantilever beam. F is the force applied. L is the
length of the beam. E is the modulus of elasticity of the beam material. I is the area
moment of inertia of the beam if bent in this direction. The deflection of the beam is
proportional to the force applied and inversely proportional to the elastic modulus and
the area moment of inertia. The deflection of the beam is proportional to the third

Stress within a material is a three-dimensional (tensor) quantity.

Stress Within a Material
In defining stress in the prior section, stress applied to a surface was discussed. This is a
two-dimensional consideration that is relatively easy to visualize. Stress also is carried
within the material that is loaded. Because the object is three-dimensional and the
material has volume, the stress within an object is defined three-dimensionally (stress is
a tensor quantity). Imagine taking a slice of an object that is being loaded and looking at
the internal stress on the plane of the cut surface. The stress on that cut surface will
depend on the direction and location of the cutting plane.
Stress Distribution Within a Beam
A beam that is bent has a tension side and a compression side.
The highest internal stresses in a bent beam are at the surfaces of the beam.
A beam that is being twisted has the highest stresses at the outer surface of the beam.

Stress Distribution Within a Beam
The stress within the material of an object that is being bent or twisted is not uniform
throughout the material. A beam that is being loaded with a bending moment has a
tension side and a compression side. A long bone can be considered as a beam. The
tension or compression side of the long bone is an important consideration in deciding
the location for placement of a plate to fix a fracture or the location for the placement of
a tension band.
Therefore, the stress within the material of the bending beam varies through the cross-
section of the beam. Imagine cutting the beam in half and looking at the material
stresses in that cutting plane. The material stress transitions from tensile stress on the
tension side to compressive stress on the compression side (Figure 10, A). The location

Internal Bone Stresses and Fracture Patterns
Fracture patterns are determined by the internal stresses in the material that are caused by
external loads.
Uniaxial tension causes a transverse fracture.
Uniaxial compression causes an oblique fracture.
Bending causes a butterfly fragment.
Torsion causes a spiral fracture.

Internal Bone Stresses and Fracture Patterns
To relate applied loading to bone fracture patterns, surgeons must first understand that
because bone is a mineralized material, it is strongest in compression, it is weakest in
tension, and it has intermediate strength in shear. Because stress is a three-dimensional
quantity, the planes of maximum tensile and compressive stress always are
perpendicular to each other, and the plane of maximum shear stress is at 45° to the
planes of maximum tensile and compressive stress. Basic fracture patterns can inform
orthopaedic surgeons on the manner in which the bone was loaded at the time of
fracture. If a bone is axially loaded in tension, the plane of maximum tensile stress is
perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the bone, and the bone fractures with a
transverse pattern (Figure 11, A).
If the bone is axially loaded in compression, very little tensile stress exists in the bone;
therefore, the next weakest plane of failure is the plane of maximum shear. This is at 45°
to the long axis of the bone if the bone is axially loaded in compression, and the bone
fractures with an oblique pattern (Figure 11, B).
If the bone is loaded in bending, the tension side breaks transversely, and the
compression side breaks at a 45° angle (the plane of maximum shear stress), resulting in
a butterfly fragment (Figure 11, C).

Fatigue depends on the stress in the material and the number of loading cycles.


Fatigue
Orthopaedic surgeons must understand the concept of fatigue because it is a common
cause of failure of orthopaedic implants (Figure 12).
Figure 12 AP radiograph of the right hip of a patient demonstrates a subtrochanteric
nonunion. Weight bearing led to fatigue fracture of the cephalomedullary nail and the
distal interlocking screw. (Image courtesy of Nicholas J. Giori, MD, PhD, Palo Alto, CA.)
The screws shown in Figure 12 did not break because they were loaded to failure
(beyond their ultimate strength) in one loading cycle. Instead, they broke because of
metal fatigue. Fatigue arises from repeated stress application to a material. If the
material has any small defect within it (all materials do, even on a nano scale), then the
defect may be a site of stress concentration. This means that the three-dimensional
tensile stress within the material is particularly concentrated at this defect and rises
above the ultimate strength of the material in a tiny volume of the material near the
defect. A tiny crack in the material can then develop at this site. With repeated loading of

the structure, the tip of the crack becomes the site of stress concentration. With every
load cycle, the crack propagates a tiny bit more. With repeated loading, the crack can
propagate across nearly the entire structure. At this point, the remaining intact material
has too small of a cross-sectional surface area to withstand even a single loading cycle,
and the implant breaks. Orthopaedic surgeons who have long been in practice have seen
not only screws and plates break but also heads of old mallets break off of their handles
because of metal fatigue.
Endurance Limit
The endurance limit is the internal material stress below which cracks do not propagate.
Stressing a material above the endurance limit will eventually lead to fatigue fracture of the
material.
Stressing a material below the endurance limit will never lead to a fatigue fracture.

Endurance Limit
A threshold of stress exists below which metal does not fatigue because the load applied
to the structure is simply too low to generate stresses, even near defects, that rise above
the ultimate strength of the material. If a giant steel beam that is used to build a
skyscraper is hit repeatedly with a feather, the steel beam would never break in fatigue.
In this scenario, the steel in the beam is not being stressed enough to form and
propagate cracks in the steel. This threshold of stress below which a material will not
fatigue is called the endurance limit. Ideally, all implants would be designed so that the
stresses in the material under physiologic load are below the endurance limit; however,
this is impossible in many circumstances because the screws or plates, for example,
would need to be too thick to be practical. Important design changes in hip
replacements have been made to reduce stress concentrations and bring the stresses in
the structure close to the endurance limit. The neck of a hip replacement stem can carry
approximately three times body weight for many millions of loading cycles over the
lifetime of the implant without breaking from fatigue. Because of design improvements
over the decades, fractured femoral stems are far less common.

Part 4: Kinematics, Kinetics, and Analysis of Human Movement
Kinematics
Kinematics is the field within classic mechanics that describes only the motion of objects—
position, velocity, and acceleration.

Kinematics
The kinetics of motion of the hip joint, for example, are relatively straightforward
because the hip can be conceptualized as a ball and socket joint. The kinetics of the knee
joint are far more complex, with components of translation and rotation in multiple
planes. In knee replacement, surgical procedures and implant designs have been
modified to attempt to achieve knee kinematics close to normal, with the hope that this
will improve subjective outcomes in patients who undergo knee replacement. Posterior
stabilized implants were designed to ensure that posterior roll back occurs reliably with
knee flexion after knee replacement. Rotating platform and medial pivot knee
replacement designs were driven by a desire to allow for more normal axial rotation at
the knee during flexion. More highly constrained knee replacement implants were
designed to limit abnormal kinematics at the knee if supporting ligaments are deficient.
Kinetics
Kinetics is the study of motion and its causes—forces and moments. Newton’s laws of motion
are the foundation of kinetics.
Newton’s laws of motion are:
1. A body that is at rest or moving at a constant speed in a straight line will remain at rest or
keep moving in a straight line at constant speed unless it is acted on by a force (Law of
inertia).
2. The time rate of change of the momentum of a body is equal in magnitude and direction to
the force imposed on it (force = mass × acceleration).

Analysis of Human Movement
Motion analysis uses the laws of physics to assess the complex three-dimensional motion of
the body.

Analysis of Human Movement
Motion analysis can be performed to assess any motion; however, it is most commonly
performed to assess gait. A motion analysis laboratory has multiple infrared or video
cameras, or even fluoroscopes, that are used to capture the kinematics of motion in
multiple planes. If kinetics are of interest, then force plates, which are commonly located
on the ground on a gait runway or on a treadmill, can be used to record ground reaction
forces. By recording three-dimensional joint position and joint angles and by measuring
a ground reaction force vector during gait, net joint forces and moments can be
calculated using inverse dynamics. Gait analysis can be used to assess pathologic gait
and plan corrective surgical treatment in patients with conditions such as cerebral palsy.
Motion analysis laboratories are commonly used in biomechanics research to assess
normal human motion and the effects of orthopaedic interventions on motion.
Restoration of knee kinematics after knee replacement is of particular interest and a
common subject of research in motion analysis laboratories.
